newsitem.title: GERMANY: Feminist Hite seeks European parliament platform.
newsitem.headline: Feminist Hite seeks European parliament platform.

text.p: Controversial feminist Shere Hite, her back firmly turned on the United States, said on Friday she wanted to defend women's rights as a member of the European parliament.
"Governments are not really taking into consideration women's rights in their foreign policy," she told Reuters at the world's largest book fair in Frankfurt.

Hite, famed for her sex research reports which said men were failing to satisfy women, has renounced her American citizenship and now has a German passport. She is married to German concert pianist Friedrich Hoericke.
She is keen to seek a political platform for her feminist views and said she has been approached by women's organisations in "two or three countries" who want her to stand for parliament.
Hite complained that, for instance: "No government has spoken out about what Iran is doing to women in its country. I find this blindness so frustrating."
For 20 years, Hite's critics have lambasted her questionnaire research methods, calling her best-selling reports "masturbation manuals."
She was even accused of being "suspiciously sexy for a feminist" as she has flowing, delicate blonde hair.
Hite says she feels more at home in Germany than the United States. "A lot of people helped me develop myself. I think the atmosphere here is much more appropriate to intellectual development."
She has no regrets about abandoning the United States.

"Like England after the so-called loss of empire, America is going through a state of transition to be one of the world's powers and not the completely dominant one. That seems to be a hard transition for any country.
"Pat Buchanan looks for a scapegoat among radical feminists. Others are burning black churches in the south."

Hite, publicising her autobiography at the Frankfurt book fair and also offering sexual counselling via the Internet, has published four reports on everything from women's sexuality to the role of the traditional family.
They sparked vitriolic criticism from the U.S. media. Some American academics call her "Sheer Hype" and one British woman writer once dubbed her works "The Hate Reports."
Hite, at ease living in what she sees as a more tolerant European society, said of the years of attacks: "I don't mind the flak about one's ideas. It is the personal vilification that is irritating."
